title: The Beginning of the Gospel
summary: Mark opens with John the Baptist preaching repentance in the wilderness and announcing a mightier one to come. Jesus is baptized, hears the Father's voice, and is driven by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tested. Then he announces the kingdom of God in Galilee, calls four fishermen, drives out an unclean spirit in the Capernaum synagogue, heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, withdraws to pray, and cleanses a leper who then spreads the news everywhere.
story:
Mark begins abruptly, with no birth story and no genealogy. His first line names his subject, “This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (verse 1), and his second reaches back to Israel's prophets, who promised that God would send a messenger to prepare his way and would then come himself to rescue his people. John is that messenger. The reader is told at the outset what the people in the story will spend the whole book struggling to see.

From there the chapter moves at a run. Within forty-five verses Jesus is baptized, named Son by the voice from heaven, driven into the wilderness, preaching in Galilee, calling fishermen, silencing an unclean spirit in a synagogue, healing a household and then a town, slipping away before dawn to pray, and touching a man no one else would touch. By the end his fame has spread so widely that he can no longer enter a town openly. The chapter lays down the book's main threads: who Jesus is, the arrival of God's kingdom, the authority with which he speaks and acts, the call to follow, and the strange silence he asks of those who know him. It also begins and ends in the wilderness, first John's and then the lonely places where Jesus is driven by the crowds, a hint that the one who came to bring God's people home will himself be pushed to the margins.
historical:
The events are set in the late 20s AD. Tiberius was emperor in Rome (AD 14 to 37), and Luke dates John's preaching to the fifteenth year of his reign (Luke 3:1), which on the usual reckoning is about AD 28 or 29. Galilee, where most of the chapter takes place, was ruled by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who held Galilee and Perea as tetrarch from 4 BC to AD 39. Judea and Jerusalem, from which the crowds go out to John (verse 5), were under a Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, from about AD 26 to 36. John the Baptist is known outside the New Testament. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the 90s, describes him as a good man who urged Jews to practice virtue, justice toward one another, and piety toward God, and to come to baptism; he says Antipas feared that John's hold on the crowds might lead to revolt and had him imprisoned and put to death at the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea (Antiquities 18.116-119). Josephus adds that when Antipas's army was destroyed by the Nabatean king Aretas IV in AD 36, some Jews saw it as God's punishment for John's death. Mark's brief note that Jesus began in Galilee ‘after John was handed over’ (verse 14) points ahead to the full story in 6:14-29.

The wilderness near the Jordan carried a long memory. Israel had crossed the Jordan into the land under Joshua (Joshua 3 to 4), and Elijah crossed it just before he was taken up (2 Kings 2:6-11). Isaiah 40:3 had pictured a road prepared in the wilderness for God's return from exile. A few miles from where the Jordan enters the Dead Sea lay the settlement of Qumran, whose community applied that same verse to itself: the Community Rule (1QS 8:13-14) explains its withdrawal into the desert as preparing the way of the Lord by the study of the law. Nothing shows that John belonged to that group, but the two shared a wilderness and a text. The Hebrew of Isaiah 40:3 attaches ‘in the wilderness’ to the command to prepare, as the BSB translates it there (“Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness”); the Greek translation, which Mark follows, attaches it to the voice. Both fit John, a voice in the wilderness calling Israel to make ready.

Capernaum, Jesus' base, was a fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about 21 kilometers (13 miles) long and 13 kilometers (8 miles) wide. It lay near the Jordan's inflow, on the border between Antipas's territory and that of his brother Philip, which is why it had a toll office (2:14). Fishing and fish-salting were major trades around the lake; the town of Magdala was known in Greek as Taricheae, from the word for salted fish. A fishing boat of the period, about eight meters long, was recovered from the mud near Ginosar in 1986. Excavations at Capernaum by the Franciscan archaeologists Virgilio Corbo and Stanislao Loffreda, beginning in 1968, found a white limestone synagogue built in the late fourth or fifth century over basalt foundations and a cobbled floor that many think belong to the first-century building, and a modest basalt house a short walk away that was turned into a place of Christian meeting, later covered by an octagonal church in the fifth century. The pilgrim Egeria, late in the fourth century, reported that Peter's house in Capernaum had been made into a church. The identifications are debated, but they confirm that the Capernaum of this chapter was a real, modest lakeside town where a synagogue and a fisherman's house stood close together, as verses 21 and 29 assume.
cultural:
John's clothing of camel's hair and a leather belt recalls Elijah, whom 2 Kings 1:8 describes as “a hairy man” with “a leather belt around his waist,” and a hairy cloak was a prophet's recognized garb (Zechariah 13:4). Malachi had promised that God would send Elijah before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5), and Mark later has Jesus identify John with that figure (9:11-13). John's food was the food of the wilderness. Locusts were among the few insects the law allowed Israel to eat (Leviticus 11:21-22), and the Damascus Document from Qumran even gives rules for preparing them (CD 12:14-15); wild honey was honey from wild bees or the sweet sap of trees. A man who lived this way stood outside the economy of the towns, dependent on what God provided.

Washing with water was part of Jewish life. The law prescribed baths for many kinds of ritual impurity (Leviticus 15), and stepped immersion pools (miqva'ot) have been excavated in Jerusalem, at Qumran, and in Galilean villages. John's baptism differed in three ways. It was administered by another person (they ‘were baptized by him’, verse 5) rather than self-immersion; it was tied to repentance and the forgiveness of sins rather than to a particular impurity; and it seems to have been done once, as a mark of a turned life, rather than repeated. Josephus stresses that John's baptism did not by itself remove sin but presupposed a soul already cleansed by right conduct; Mark stresses repentance and forgiveness. Both agree that the rite required a changed life. The Babylonian Talmud records a saying that a disciple should do for his teacher every task a slave does for his master except untying his sandal (Ketubbot 96a); if that attitude was current in John's day, John claims to be unworthy of the one task too low even for a disciple.

Disciples in this world usually chose their teacher. The Mishnah preserves the sage Joshua ben Perahiah's counsel to provide oneself with a teacher (Avot 1:6), and disciples of the rabbis sought out a master and asked to learn from him. Jesus reverses the pattern: he calls, and the fishermen come. The closest model is Elijah casting his cloak over Elisha at the plow (1 Kings 19:19-21), but Elisha asked leave to kiss his parents goodbye, and the brothers here ask nothing. Leaving Zebedee ‘in the boat with the hired men’ (verse 20) shows a family business large enough to employ workers, and leaving it would have been a costly break with a father in a society where sons carried on the family trade and cared for their parents.

The synagogue was the village's meeting place for reading and teaching the law and the prophets on the Sabbath, and a visiting teacher could be invited to speak (Luke 4:16-17, Acts 13:15). The Theodotus inscription from Jerusalem, usually dated before AD 70, describes a synagogue built for reading the law and teaching the commandments. The scribes taught by handing on the rulings of earlier authorities, a method the later Mishnah displays on every page. Jewish exorcists of the period worked with incantations, names, and objects: Josephus tells of an exorcist named Eleazar who drew a demon out through a man's nostrils with a ring and incantations attributed to Solomon, in the presence of Vespasian (Antiquities 8.46-49). Jesus uses no ritual; he speaks a command. The Jewish day ran from sunset to sunset, and carrying burdens from one place to another was forbidden on the Sabbath (Jeremiah 17:21-22; the Mishnah lists it among the thirty-nine kinds of work, Shabbat 7:2), which is why the town waits until ‘after sunset’ (verse 32) to carry its sick to the door.

The man in verse 40 had one of the skin diseases the law calls tsara'at (Leviticus 13 to 14), a term that covers several conditions, not only what is now called Hansen's disease. The law required such a person to tear his clothes, cover his mouth, cry ‘Unclean, unclean’, and live outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45-46), and anyone who touched him became unclean. The disease was felt as a kind of living death: Aaron pleads that Miriam not be like a stillborn child (Numbers 12:12), and the Babylonian Talmud counts the one with tsara'at among four who are regarded as dead (Nedarim 64b). Healing it was thought to be God's work alone; when Naaman arrived for cleansing, the king of Israel asked whether he was God, to kill and to make alive (2 Kings 5:7). A cleansed person was examined by a priest and offered the sacrifices of Leviticus 14 before rejoining the community, which is the ‘offering Moses prescribed’ of verse 44.
literary:
Mark's opening is compressed and quick. The Greek euthys, ‘immediately’ or ‘at once’, appears eleven times in this chapter and more than forty times in the Gospel, and Mark often narrates in the present tense (literally ‘they go into Capernaum’, verse 21), so the story feels as if it were happening in front of the reader. The prologue tells the reader who Jesus is before any character knows, and scholars debate whether it ends at verse 13 or at verse 15. The case for 15 is that the word gospel frames the section, standing in verse 1 and again in verses 14 and 15, so that the first thing the Gospel reports Jesus saying is the gospel the title promised.

The chapter is built in movements. The prologue (1 to 15) holds three scenes in the wilderness: John's preaching, the baptism, and the testing. Then comes the call of the first disciples (16 to 20), which opens the Galilean ministry exactly as the next two sections of the Gospel open with the disciples (3:13-19 and 6:7-13). Verses 21 to 39 describe what readers call a day in Capernaum: a Sabbath that runs from the synagogue in the morning, to Simon's house at midday, to the whole town at the door after sunset, to prayer in the dark before dawn. The chapter closes with the cleansing of the leper (40 to 45), a single encounter that ends with Jesus unable to enter a town. The word wilderness or lonely place (erēmos) appears six times, at the beginning (verses 3, 4, 12, 13) and at the end (35, 45), framing the whole.

Two patterns run through the chapter and the book. The first is the command to silence. Jesus silences the unclean spirit (verse 25), forbids the demons to speak ‘because they knew who He was’ (verse 34), and sternly orders the cleansed leper to tell no one (verse 44). The second is irony. The verb to preach or proclaim (kēryssō) is used of John (verses 4 and 7), of Jesus (14, 38, 39), and finally of the cleansed leper, who ‘went out and openly began to proclaim’ (verse 45): the man told to be silent becomes the chapter's last preacher, and his preaching drives Jesus out into the lonely places the leper had just left. The only characters in the chapter who name Jesus correctly are the voice from heaven and the unclean spirits; the human beings are drawn to him without yet knowing who he is.

doctrines.note: Jesus' first words announce that “The time is fulfilled” and “the kingdom of God is near” (verse 15). The kingdom is God's reign arriving in the person and work of Jesus. The exorcisms and healings that follow show what that reign does as it breaks into a world held by evil, sickness, and exclusion: it drives out what destroys and restores people to their community.

At the baptism the Son comes up from the water, the Spirit descends on him, and the Father speaks from heaven (verses 10 and 11). Mark does not develop a doctrine, but the scene became one of the church's key texts for confessing one God in three persons, and the Eastern churches call the feast that celebrates it the Theophany, the appearing of God.

Mark names Jesus the Christ, the anointed king, in his first verse, and the Father's words echo the royal decree of Psalm 2:7 and the servant of Isaiah 42:1. The anointing with the Spirit at the Jordan is the Messiah's commissioning; the rest of the book shows that this king will serve, suffer, and give his life (10:45).

John preaches “a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (verse 4), and Jesus calls, “Repent and believe in the gospel” (verse 15). Repentance (metanoia) is a turning of the whole life toward God, joined here to trust in good news. The fishermen who leave their nets show what that turning looks like in practice.

The chapter sets Jesus against the powers of evil from the start. He is tested by Satan in the wilderness while angels serve him (verse 13), and in the synagogue an unclean spirit recognizes him and fears destruction (verse 24). Mark presents these powers as real but subordinate: they know who Jesus is, and they obey his word.

words.note: Euangelion, gospel, good news. It occurs about seventy-six times in the New Testament, most often in Paul, and seven times in Mark, three of them in this chapter (verses 1, 14, 15). In the Greek world the word could announce a military victory or the birth or accession of an emperor; the calendar inscription from Priene (9 BC) says the birthday of Augustus was the beginning of good news for the world. In the Greek Old Testament the related verb describes the messenger who announces that God reigns (Isaiah 52:7). BDAG describes its Christian sense as the good news of God's saving action in Jesus. Mark uses the noun both for the book's subject (verse 1) and for the message Jesus proclaims (verse 14).

Euthys (and its twin eutheōs), immediately, at once. Mark uses it about forty times, more than the rest of the New Testament together, and eleven times in this chapter. Sometimes it means only next or then, and translators vary it for that reason, but its frequency gives the story its pace and its sense that with Jesus God's long-awaited action has arrived without delay.

Basileia, kingdom, reign. It occurs about 160 times in the New Testament; the phrase kingdom of God appears fourteen times in Mark, first here in verse 15. It means God's royal rule more than a territory, the reign the prophets had promised (Isaiah 52:7, Daniel 2:44, 7:14). Jesus says it has come near (ēngiken, a perfect tense), and scholars debate whether that means it is at hand but still future or already arriving; Mark's narrative, in which the kingdom is visible in Jesus' acts, suggests both.

Metanoeō, to repent. It occurs thirty-four times in the New Testament and twice in Mark (1:15, 6:12); the noun metanoia occurs once in Mark, in verse 4. Its ordinary Greek sense is to change one's mind, but in the Gospels it carries the weight of the Hebrew prophets' call to turn or return (shuv) to God, a change of direction in life, not only regret. Repentance and faith are joined as two sides of one response in verse 15.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. It occurs about 102 times in the New Testament and ten times in Mark, twice in this chapter (verses 22 and 27). The crowd notices two things: Jesus teaches with authority, not as the scribes, and his word is obeyed by unclean spirits. The same word returns when he claims authority to forgive sins (2:10) and when the temple leaders ask by what authority he acts (11:28).

Akathartos, unclean, impure. It occurs thirty-two times in the New Testament and eleven times in Mark, where it almost always describes spirits. The phrase unclean spirit joins the language of the purity laws to the world of demons: these powers defile and exclude. It matters that the first exorcism happens in a synagogue on the Sabbath, the place and day of Israel's holiness, and that the spirit calls Jesus ‘the Holy One of God’ (verse 24).

Schizō, to split, tear. It occurs eleven times in the New Testament and twice in Mark: here the heavens are ‘breaking open’ at the baptism (verse 10), and in 15:38 the temple curtain is torn in two at Jesus' death. Matthew and Luke use the gentler verb for opening. Mark's violent word echoes the prayer of Isaiah 64:1, “If only You would rend the heavens and come down,” and the two tearings frame the Gospel, each followed by the naming of Jesus as God's Son.

Splanchnizomai, to be moved with compassion, from splanchna, the inner organs felt as the seat of emotion. It occurs twelve times in the New Testament, only in the first three Gospels, always of Jesus or of a figure in his parables who stands for God (the father of the prodigal, the good Samaritan, the forgiving master). Mark uses it four times (1:41, 6:34, 8:2, 9:22). In verse 41 a few manuscripts read that Jesus was angered instead; see the note on the text.

christ:
Mark's first verse tells the reader who Jesus is: the Christ, the anointed king Israel awaited, and the Son of God. The Father confirms it at the baptism in words that gather three Old Testament voices: Psalm 2:7, where God calls the king “My Son”; Isaiah 42:1, where God's servant is the one “in whom My soul delights” and on whom God puts his Spirit; and perhaps Genesis 22:2, where the Greek Old Testament calls Isaac Abraham's beloved son, the son he is asked to offer. King, servant, and beloved son: the voice from heaven names in advance the path the Gospel will walk, from royal authority to a servant's death.

The opening quotation makes a still larger claim. Isaiah 40:3 calls for a way prepared for the LORD, Israel's God, and Malachi 3:1 promises a messenger sent ahead of the Lord who will come to his temple. Mark applies both to John as forerunner and to Jesus as the one who comes. Rikki Watts (Isaiah's New Exodus in Mark, 1997) and Richard Hays (Echoes of Scripture in the Gospels, 2016) argue that Mark thereby presents Jesus' coming as the coming of Israel's God himself, the long-promised return of the Lord to his people. The torn heavens answer Isaiah's prayer that God would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). Jewish texts preserved in the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, a work with a complicated history of Jewish composition and Christian editing, speak of the heavens opening over a coming priest or king and the Spirit resting on him (Testament of Levi 18:6-7; Testament of Judah 24:2); whatever the date of those lines, they show the hope Mark's scene fulfills.

Jesus is then driven into the wilderness for forty days, recalling Israel's forty years of testing (Deuteronomy 8:2), Moses' forty days on the mountain (Exodus 34:28), and Elijah's forty days' walk to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). Mark, unlike Matthew and Luke, does not narrate the temptations or their outcome; he says only that Jesus was tempted by Satan, was with the wild animals, and was served by angels. Richard Bauckham has read the wild animals as a picture of Eden's peace restored in the new Adam (compare Isaiah 11:6, “The wolf will live with the lamb”), while others read them as the dangers of the desert from which God protects his servant (Psalm 91:11-13). Either way the Son enters the place of Israel's testing and of humanity's enmity with creation, and heaven attends him there.

The rest of the chapter shows the Son at work. He announces God's reign, calls people to follow him personally, speaks with an authority that needs no citation, and commands unclean spirits, who recognize him as the Holy One of God. John had promised one ‘more powerful’ (verse 7), and Jesus will later describe his work as binding the strong man (3:27). He takes a feverish woman by the hand and raises her (the verb, egeirō, is the one the angel will use at the tomb, 16:6), and she serves. He rises before dawn to pray, and he explains that preaching is “why I have come” (verse 38), a phrase Simon Gathercole (The Preexistent Son, 2006) reads as a hint that Jesus came from somewhere, though many interpreters take it to mean only that he came out from Capernaum. Finally he touches a man with a defiling disease, and instead of the uncleanness passing to Jesus, cleanness passes to the man. By the chapter's end the healed leper is inside the town and Jesus must stay out in the lonely places, a small picture of the exchange Mark will show fully at the cross.

Some early manuscripts lack the words ‘the Son of God’ in verse 1, but the title stands at the Gospel's decisive points: the voice at the baptism (1:11), the voice at the transfiguration (9:7), and the centurion at the cross, “Truly this man was the Son of God” (15:39). Mark's portrait is of one person who is both the Father's beloved Son and a man who prays in the dark, touches the sick, and will be handed over as John was.
interpretation:
The opening of Mark shaped the Gospel's symbol. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies 3.11.8, around 180) gave Mark the eagle, because the Gospel begins with the prophetic Spirit descending from on high in the words of Isaiah. Jerome, in the preface to his Commentary on Matthew (398), gave Mark instead the lion, because the book opens with a voice roaring in the wilderness, and his assignment became the church's. The fathers wrote little on Mark as a book, but they wrote a great deal on this chapter's events through the parallels in Matthew and Luke. Verse 2 drew the first outside attack on the chapter: the pagan philosopher Porphyry, in the third century, cited it as proof that the evangelists did not know their own Scriptures, since Mark ascribes to Isaiah a line from Malachi. Jerome answered him in his Letter 57 to Pammachius (395), arguing that Mark set a line of Malachi before Isaiah's words as an introductory reference and named the prophet whose text he goes on to expound. The Irish monk Cummian (around 610), Bede (early eighth century), and Theophylact of Ohrid (late eleventh century) read the chapter verse by verse, and Thomas Aquinas gathered patristic comment on it in the Catena Aurea.

Two debates of the early church turned on verses 9 to 11. Some second-century Christians read the baptism as the moment the man Jesus was adopted as Son: Theodotus, a leather-worker from Byzantium teaching in Rome, was excommunicated by Bishop Victor in the 190s for holding that Jesus became Christ when the Spirit came upon him at the Jordan. The church answered that the voice declares an existing sonship rather than creating one. The scene also became a primary text for the Trinity: the Son in the water, the Spirit descending, the Father's voice. The Eastern churches celebrate the baptism on January 6 as the Theophany and bless the waters that day; in the West the Baptism of the Lord closes the Christmas season. The Reformers used the chapter to talk about the relation between John's baptism and Christian baptism; Calvin (Institutes 4.15.7) argued that the two are the same baptism, John baptizing in the name of the one who was to come and the apostles in the name of the one who had come, while Anabaptist and later Baptist readers stressed John's call to repent as the condition of the rite. Those debates continue.

Modern scholarship made this chapter a proving ground for its methods. Willi Marxsen (1956) argued that Mark's Galilee is a theological place as much as a geographical one, the place of revelation and of the risen Lord's appearing (14:28, 16:7). Leander Keck (New Testament Studies, 1966) argued that the prologue runs through verse 15. Rikki Watts (1997) read the opening quotation as the key to the whole book, a new exodus led by Israel's returning God, and Richard Hays (2016) developed that into a case for a Christology of divine identity in Mark. Joel Marcus's commentary (2000) set the chapter against the Dead Sea Scrolls, and Bart Ehrman's Orthodox Corruption of Scripture (1993) used the text of verses 1 and 11 in other Gospels to show how Christological debates left their mark on the manuscripts.

The chapter fills the lectionaries. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year B, verses 1 to 8 are read on the Second Sunday of Advent, verses 4 to 11 on the Baptism of the Lord, verses 9 to 15 on the First Sunday in Lent, and the rest of the chapter on the Sundays after Epiphany (14 to 20, 21 to 28, 29 to 39, and 40 to 45). In art the baptism is one of the oldest and most repeated subjects, from the catacombs to Piero della Francesca's Baptism of Christ (probably 1440s, now in the National Gallery, London) and the Baptism of Christ by Andrea del Verrocchio and his pupil Leonardo da Vinci (about 1470 to 1475, Uffizi), in which the young Leonardo painted one of the kneeling angels. Duccio's small panel of the Calling of Peter and Andrew, painted for the Maestà altarpiece in Siena (1308 to 1311) and now in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, shows Christ on the shore and the two brothers in a boat on a gold sea.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter, and the chapter is also where the earliest surviving fragment of Mark, P137 (late second or early third century), preserves a few words of verses 7 to 9 and 16 to 18.

Verse 1: the words ‘the Son of God’ are missing from the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, from Codex Koridethi, and from Origen's quotations of the verse, and present in Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, Codex Washingtonianus, a corrector of Sinaiticus, and most later manuscripts. The Nestle-Aland edition prints them in brackets and the SBL Greek New Testament omits them. Bart Ehrman argues that scribes added them; Tommy Wasserman (Journal of Theological Studies, 2011) argues that they are original and were lost by accident in a line of abbreviated sacred names. Most English versions print the words, some with a note.

Verse 2: the earliest manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, read ‘in Isaiah the prophet’, though the first line comes from Malachi 3:1 (with the wording of Exodus 23:20 in the Greek). Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘in the prophets’, a correction that removes the difficulty. The harder reading is almost certainly original. A few manuscripts add ‘before you’ at the end of the verse, from Matthew and Luke.

Verse 14: the Byzantine manuscripts and the KJV read ‘the gospel of the kingdom of God’ where the earlier manuscripts read ‘the gospel of God’. Verse 34: several manuscripts, including Vaticanus, add that the demons knew him ‘to be the Christ’, probably from Luke 4:41. Verse 41: most manuscripts read splanchnistheis, ‘moved with compassion’, but Codex Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts read orgistheis, ‘becoming angry’. The NIV (2011) renders ‘indignant’ and the SBL edition prints ‘angry’; Ehrman defended that reading in an essay titled ‘A Leper in the Hands of an Angry Jesus’, and Peter J. Williams (Novum Testamentum, 2012) answered that the two Greek words look alike enough for an accidental change and that the witnesses for anger are few and related. Most versions keep compassion.

Versification: two Old Testament texts behind this chapter are numbered differently in Hebrew and English Bibles. The promise of Elijah's return, Malachi 4:5 in English Bibles, is Malachi 3:23 in the Hebrew Bible, which has no chapter 4. The prayer that God would rend the heavens, Isaiah 64:1 in English Bibles, is Isaiah 63:19b in Hebrew. Readers comparing a Jewish translation with an English Christian Bible will find the same words under different numbers.

teach.big: The long-promised Lord has come in Jesus, the beloved Son anointed with the Spirit, and his arrival means that God's reign is near, calling people to turn and follow and reaching even those the community keeps outside.

outline.t: The good news begins where the prophets left off: God keeps his word by sending a messenger, and John's whole greatness is that he points past himself to one more powerful.
Jesus stands with sinners in the water, and heaven tears open to declare who he is: the beloved Son on whom the Spirit rests, the king and servant in one.
The same Spirit drives the Son into the place of testing; before he rescues anyone from Satan's grip, he faces Satan himself, and God's servants attend him.
Jesus' message in one sentence: God's appointed time has come, his reign has drawn near, so turn around and trust the good news.
Following Jesus begins with his call, not our application, and it costs real things: nets, boats, a family business, a father in the boat.
Jesus' word carries its own authority, in teaching and against the powers that destroy people, and even in the synagogue evil has to reckon with him.
The kingdom comes into ordinary homes: a sick woman raised to serve, and a whole town brought to the door; the demons' testimony is refused because the truth about Jesus is not theirs to tell.
Surrounded by demand, Jesus withdraws to pray and then moves on, because his purpose is set by the Father's mission, not by the crowd's agenda.
Jesus touches the untouchable and makes him clean, restores him to his community through the law's own process, and takes the outsider's place himself.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common. The first treats the chapter as a list of miracles meant to prove that Jesus is powerful, and so misses what the power is for: each act restores a person to God's people (the possessed man in the synagogue, the mother-in-law to her household, the leper to the town). The second turns verses 16 to 20 into a general lesson on dropping everything for a career in ministry. The call is real and costly, but the fishermen are called to follow Jesus, and many whom Jesus helps in Mark are sent back to their homes and towns (5:19); preaching should not imply that faithful discipleship always means leaving one's work.

A third pitfall is to explain away the demons as primitive language for illness. Mark distinguishes the sick from the demon-possessed (verse 34), and the text presents real powers opposed to God; teachers can acknowledge the modern questions without flattening the text. A fourth is to make John's diet and clothing into a model of spiritual heroism, when Mark uses them to identify him with Elijah. A fifth, common in quick readings of verse 41, is to preach a Jesus of mild sentiment; whether the text says compassion or anger, the Jesus of this chapter is intensely engaged with suffering and with what causes it. Finally, avoid treating the commands to silence as a strategy for publicity (tell no one, so everyone will hear): Mark presents the leper's disobedience as the reason Jesus could no longer enter a town.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on people who live with chronic illness, disability, or a condition that separates them from others, and on those who carry shame about their bodies. The leper's words, “If You are willing, You can make me clean” (verse 40), voice a doubt about God's willingness more than his power, and many in any congregation share it. Teach Jesus' answer with care: his willingness is shown first in his touch, before any healing. Be careful not to imply that faith guarantees physical healing; Mark himself notes that Jesus healed ‘many’, left the crowds still looking for him, and moved on (verses 34 to 38), and the Gospel as a whole leads to a cross. For people exhausted by caregiving or by others' demands, verse 35 gives permission to withdraw and pray, and verse 38 shows that Jesus did not accept the crowd's expectations as his calling.

hard.q: Why does Jesus keep telling demons and the people he heals to be silent about him?
hard.a:
The objection is that the commands make little sense as history. Jesus heals in public before crowds, yet orders the healed to tell no one; he silences demons who speak the truth about him; and the leper disobeys at once (verse 45). In 1901 William Wrede argued in The Messianic Secret in the Gospels that the pattern was not a memory of Jesus at all but a device of Mark or his tradition: the early church believed Jesus was the Messiah, knew he had not been publicly recognized as such in his lifetime, and explained the gap by projecting a secret back into the story. Rudolf Bultmann and many form critics followed him, and skeptical readers have taken the pattern as evidence that Mark's portrait of Jesus is a post-Easter construction. Jewish readers have added a sharper form of the question: if Jesus hid his claims, can the charge that he claimed to be Messiah be fairly laid against his own people for not accepting it?

Responses have taken several forms. James D. G. Dunn (Tyndale Bulletin, 1970) argued that much of the secrecy has a historical origin in Jesus' own caution. In a land where messianic claims could spark revolt and Roman reprisal, Jesus avoided being taken for a political liberator, and he refused the testimony of demons, whose confession was not faith and whose timing he would not accept. Others note that the commands fall mostly on healings and exorcisms, where crowds seeking wonders could make preaching impossible, as verse 45 shows. Still others, including many who accept part of Wrede's analysis, read the secrecy as Mark's theology built on real tradition: Jesus' identity could not be rightly understood until the cross and resurrection defined what kind of Messiah he was, which is why, after the transfiguration, he tells the disciples to tell no one ‘until the Son of Man had risen from the dead’ (9:9). The essays gathered by Christopher Tuckett in The Messianic Secret (1983) show how scholars have mixed these explanations. The silence is lifted in Mark only when Jesus himself answers the high priest (14:61-62) and when a Gentile soldier speaks at the cross.

hard.q: Does the baptism make Jesus the Son of God, or does it announce what he already was?
hard.a:
The objection is that Mark, the earliest Gospel, has no birth story and no preexistence prologue, and that his first scene with Jesus is one in which the Spirit comes upon him and a voice says ‘You are My beloved Son’. Read alone, that looks like an appointment. In the late second century Theodotus of Byzantium taught in Rome that Jesus was a man on whom the Spirit came at the Jordan, and Bishop Victor excommunicated him for it. Some modern critics hold that Mark's Christology is close to this: Bart Ehrman (How Jesus Became God, 2014) argues that early Christians first thought Jesus was exalted to divine sonship at his resurrection, and then pushed the moment back to the baptism, as Mark does, and later to his birth and before creation. Jewish scholars add that Son of God in the Hebrew Bible is a royal and covenant title (Psalm 2:7, 2 Samuel 7:14, Exodus 4:22) that never implied divinity, and Adela Yarbro Collins and John J. Collins (King and Messiah as Son of God, 2008) trace how the title was used of Israel's king and of the Messiah.

Responses come from several directions. Many note that the voice speaks in the present tense (‘You are’), not the language of appointment, and that the verb of delight (eudokēsa, an aorist) can express a settled, existing pleasure. Rikki Watts and Richard Hays argue that Mark's opening identification of Jesus with the LORD of Isaiah 40:3 and Malachi 3:1, whose way is prepared, places Jesus within the identity of Israel's God before the baptism is described, and Simon Gathercole (The Preexistent Son, 2006) argues that Jesus' ‘I have come’ sayings in Mark (1:38, 2:17, 10:45) imply that he came from elsewhere. Larry Hurtado (Lord Jesus Christ, 2003) argues from the worship of Jesus in the earliest churches that a high view of him was early, not late. The church's confession, fixed at Nicaea (325), is that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and that the baptism reveals and anoints him for his mission; Christians who share that confession still differ in how much of it they think Mark himself makes explicit, and Mark's reader is left to discover through the whole story what kind of Son this is.

observe: Trace the word wilderness or solitary place through the chapter (verses 3, 4, 12, 13, 35, 45). Who goes there, and why?
Who in this chapter correctly names who Jesus is, and how does Jesus respond to each of them?
What does each person Jesus meets in verses 16 to 45 lose, gain, or do as a result?
interpret: Why might Mark begin with Isaiah and Malachi rather than with Jesus' birth? What does the opening quotation say about who is coming?
The heavens are ‘breaking open’ at the baptism and the temple curtain is torn at the cross (15:38). How do the two scenes interpret each other?
Why does Jesus refuse the demons' testimony even though what they say is true?
apply: The first disciples left nets, a boat, and a father. What would following Jesus require you to leave, or to hold more loosely, and what would it not require?
Jesus withdrew to pray when everyone was looking for him. What does your pattern of work and prayer say about whose agenda is shaping your days?
The leper doubted Jesus' willingness more than his power. Where do you believe God can help but doubt that he wants to, and what does Jesus' touch say to that doubt?
